claims.claim: No IFNγ release was obtained for the putative neo-splicetope RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 using TCR20967A2-transduced T cells co-cultured with Mel21a cells expressing a triple RAC2P29L1-45 45mer polypeptide minigene.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5B, no IFNγ release was obtained for the putative neo-splicetope RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 using TCR20967A2-transduced T cells, while peptide-loaded Mel21a cells were readily recognized and IFNγ production demonstrated the target specificity of the TCR.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Despite the overexpression of the RAC2P29L1-45 45mer substrate peptide, the authors failed to verify the in vivo generation of the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 peptide.
claims.source: Thus, despite the overexpression of the RAC2P29L1-45 45mer substrate peptide, we failed to verify the in vivo generation of the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 peptide.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative experimental results with overexpression constructs.

claims.claim: Mel21a cells transduced to express a triple RAC2P29L1-45 45mer or RAC2P29L cDNA were readily recognized by T cells transduced with TCR22894 (linear RAC2P29L-specific TCR).
claims.source: Because Mel21a cells, transduced to express a triple RAC2P29L1-45 45mer (Figure 5B) or RAC2P29L cDNA (Figure 5C), were readily recognized by T cells transduced with TCR22894, we could exclude that our inability to detect cell surface expression of the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 peptide was due to defects in the antigen presentation pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: The non-spliced RAC2P29L neoepitope (derived from RAC2P29L1-45 45mer as well as cDNA) was efficiently presented by NIH-HHD cells.
claims.source: As observed in Mel21a cells, the non-spliced RAC2P29L neoepitope (derived from RAC2P29L1-45 45mer as well as cDNA) was efficiently presented also by NIH-HHD cells, excluding potential differences in the catalytic properties of mouse and human proteasomes (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The spliced peptide-specific TCR20967A2 did not confer any reactivity to T cells upon co-culture without prior peptide loading of the target cells or overexpression of the spliced epitope.
claims.source: More importantly, again the spliced peptide-specific TCR20967A2 did not confer any reactivity to T cells upon co-culture without prior peptide loading of the target cells or overexpression of the spliced epitope (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claims.claim: RAC2P29L1-45 45mer polypeptide minigene is expressed almost fivefold higher than the RAC2P29L triple epitope spliced nonamer in mouse NIH-HHD cells.
claims.source: Quantitative PCR analysis of the triple RAC2P29L1-45 45mer polypeptide minigene and RAC2P29L triple epitope spliced nonamer expressed in mouse NIH-HHD cells revealed that RAC2P29L1-45 45mer polypeptide minigene is expressed almost fivefold higher than the RAC2P29L triple epitope spliced nonamer (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Even if the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 neo-splicetope is derived from an overexpressed substrate protein, its amounts are negligible and insufficient to allow its recognition by T cells.
claims.source: However, they clearly demonstrate that even if the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 neo-splicetope is derived from an overexpressed substrate protein, its amounts are negligible and insufficient to allow its recognition by T cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative experimental results with overexpression constructs.

claims.claim: In vitro generation of spliced epitopes by PCPS may not exhibit the same fidelity and does not always simulate the efficacy of in vivo spliced epitope generation.
claims.source: Thus, quite in contrast to the experience resulting from proteasome-dependent processing of non-spliced epitopes in vitro, in vitro generation of spliced epitopes by PCPS may not exhibit the same fidelity and does not always simulate the efficacy of in vivo spliced epitope generation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results.

claims.claim: In vitro PCPS even when combined with peptide binding and TAP transport assays are not sufficient for the prediction of immune relevance of neo-splicetopes.
claims.source: Reconsidering the workflow for the identification of neo-splicetopes, it thus seems that in vitro PCPS even when combined with peptide binding and TAP transport assays are not sufficient for the prediction of their immune relevance.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative experimental results.

claims.claim: It is mandatory to first prove the cell surface presentation of algorithm-predicted candidate neo-splicetopes before TCR generation.
claims.source: We therefore believe that it is mandatory to first prove the cell surface presentation of algorithm-predicted candidate neo-splicetopes, either in humanized mice under conditions requiring processing and presentation or by peptide elution experiments, before TCR generation.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' experimental findings.

claims.claim: The frequency of spliced epitopes is largely overestimated.
claims.source: Our data also support the notion (Mylonas et al., 2018) that the frequency of spliced epitopes is largely overestimated.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative experimental results, supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The amount of cell surface-presented spliced epitope seems to be considerably less than initially estimated.
claims.source: Thus, in light of recent reports (Mylonas et al., 2018; Rolfs et al., 2019) the amount of cell surface-presented spliced epitope seems to be considerably less than initially estimated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claims.claim: The abundance of spliced epitopes presented at the cell surface is a matter of substantial controversy.
claims.source: Although in these cases the generation efficiency of spliced epitopes in in vitro PCPS assays seemed to be in line with the in vivo situation, it should be noted, however, that the abundance of spliced epitopes presented at the cell surface is a matter of substantial controversy (Liepe et al., 2016; Liepe et al., 2019; Mylonas et al., 2018; Paes et al., 2019; Rolfs et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple papers with differing views.

claims.claim: High-quality peptide synthesis reaches a purity of 95–99% at most.
claims.source: Because high-quality peptide synthesis reaches a purity of 95–99% at most, a thorough substrate analysis appears essential to avoid false-positive results in in vitro PCPS experiments, particularly for chemically difficult substrates.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about peptide synthesis quality.

claims.claim: Even minor amounts of faulty peptide substrates will become prevalent in in vitro splicing reactions because the generation of spliced peptides is significantly less efficient than that of non-spliced peptides.
claims.source: Considering that in general the generation of spliced peptides is significantly less efficient than that of non-spliced peptides (Figure 4A), even minor amounts of faulty peptide substrates will become prevalent in in vitro splicing reactions (see also Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on relative generation efficiency.

claims.claim: High substrate and proteasome concentration used for in vitro PCPS may force splicing reactions that do either not or only inefficiently occur under in vivo conditions.
claims.source: One possible explanation for the failure to verify the in vitro PCPS reaction for RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 in in vivo settings could be the high substrate and proteasome concentration as used for in vitro PCPS, thereby forcing splicing reactions that do either not or only inefficiently occur under in vivo conditions where only a single substrate protein enters the catalytic cavity of the proteasome for processing at a given time.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results.

claims.claim: Epitope generation efficiency of both non-spliced and spliced epitopes is determined by the sequence of the epitope, its surrounding protein sequence, and connected with the cleavage site usage and cleavage strength of proteasomes.
claims.source: In addition to substrate amounts and protein turnover rates, epitope generation efficiency of both non-spliced and spliced epitopes is determined by the sequence of the epitope, its surrounding protein sequence, and connected with the cleavage site usage and cleavage strength of proteasomes (Mishto et al., 2014; Niedermann et al., 1995; Sijts and Kloetzel, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Algorithms predicting proteasomal generation of immune-relevant non-spliced epitopes still do not reach prediction efficiencies sufficient for large-scale 'reverse immunology' approaches.
claims.source: However, due to the complexity of protein sequences and lacking information on cleavage strength that decisively determines epitope generation efficiency, algorithms predicting proteasomal generation of immune-relevant non-spliced epitopes still do not reach prediction efficiencies sufficient for large-scale 'reverse immunology' approaches (Calis et al., 2015; Di Carluccio et al., 2018; Singh and Mishra, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Prediction algorithms for spliced epitopes based on protein sequence and proteasomal cleavage properties do not yet exist.
claims.source: Prediction algorithms for spliced epitopes, which are based on protein sequence and proteasomal cleavage properties, do not even yet exist.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claims.claim: In vitro generation of epitopes using purified 20S proteasomes and synthetic polypeptide substrates in combination with mass spectrometric analyses and both in vitro and in vivo CD8+ T cell assays represents the most frequently used tool to validate the generation of immune-relevant non-spliced peptides.
claims.source: Therefore, in vitro generation of epitopes using purified 20S proteasomes and synthetic polypeptide substrates encompassing the epitope(s) of interest, in combination with mass spectrometric analyses and both in vitro and in vivo CD8+ T cell assays, still represents the most frequently used tool to validate the generation of immune-relevant non-spliced peptides, assuming that it closely simulates the in vivo (in cellulo) situation with respect to both quality and relative amounts of the epitope (Kessler et al., 2001; Kessler and Melief, 2007; Sijts and Kloetzel, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing standard methodology.

results.result: TCRs specific for algorithm-predicted KRASG12V neo-splicetopes (sp1 and sp2) were successfully generated in ABabDII mice and demonstrated high functional avidity (up to 10^-10 M peptide concentration) when tested against synthetic peptides in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C16-C21 collectively demonstrate successful TCR generation against predicted KRASG12V neo-splicetopes using a humanized mouse model. The experimental data (Figures 1A-D) show robust CD8+ T cell responses, successful TCR isolation, and high functional avidity with IFNγ release at very low peptide concentrations. The cross-reactivity data (C21) is also well-documented.

results.result: KRASG12V splice-specific TCRs failed to recognize cancer cells endogenously expressing mutant KRASG12V or cells overexpressing the KRASG12V1-35 substrate, despite recognizing peptide-loaded cells and cells expressing the spliced epitope directly, indicating the predicted neo-splicetope is either not generated in vivo or produced at insufficient amounts.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C28 provide strong converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (Figures 2, 3B-E) showing that while TCRs recognize synthetic peptides and directly expressed epitopes, they fail to recognize endogenously processed antigen. The qPCR data (C27) confirms substrate expression, and the negative results despite overexpression (C26, C28) strongly support the conclusion that in vivo generation is absent or insufficient.

results.result: TCR1376 exhibits cross-reactivity with HLA-C*07 alleles (C*07:01 and C*07:02), recognizing these molecules independently of peptide loading, in addition to its intended specificity for sp1 peptide bound to HLA-A*02:01.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are well-supported by experimental data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C) showing TCR1376 recognition of multiple B-LCLs expressing HLA-C*07 and K562 cells transduced with HLA-C*07:01/02 without peptide loading. This represents an important off-target reactivity finding that would preclude therapeutic use of this TCR.

results.result: Immunization of ABabDII mice with adenovirus expressing the KRASG12V1-35 triple minigene failed to induce CD8+ T cell responses to either linear or spliced epitopes, suggesting the KRASG12V mutation is not immunogenic in the context of HLA-A*02:01.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 are supported by experimental data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) showing no IFNγ response to any of the tested epitopes after multiple immunizations. This negative result is consistent with the lack of in vivo recognition observed in other experiments and supports the broader conclusion about lack of immunogenicity.

results.result: Initial in vitro PCPS experiments appeared to generate predicted KRASG12V spliced peptides from KRASG12V2-14 and KRASG12V2-21 substrates, but subsequent analysis revealed that synthesis errors in the hydrophobic KRAS substrates produced faulty polypeptides mimicking splicing products. Using a clean KRASG12V1-21 substrate, no predicted neo-splicetopes were detected.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C39 describe a critical methodological finding supported by mass spectrometry data (Figures 3—figure supplements 3-5, Supplementary file 2). The discovery that peptide synthesis errors created false-positive splicing products (C37) and the subsequent negative results with clean substrate (C39) provide strong evidence that the initially observed KRASG12V splicing was artifactual. This represents rigorous self-correction.

results.result: The spliced RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 peptide was identified in in vitro PCPS reactions, generated via a multi-step process involving a larger precursor peptide (RAC2P29L28-34/36-40), though approximately 200-fold less efficiently than the non-spliced RAC2P29L28-36 neoepitope.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 are well-supported by mass spectrometry data (Figures 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing identification of the spliced peptide, its precursor, and kinetic analysis. The quantitative comparison of generation efficiency (C44) and mechanistic insight into the multi-step process (C45-C46) provide strong evidence for in vitro generation, though with important caveats about efficiency.

results.result: TCR20967A2 specific for the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 neo-splicetope failed to recognize cells overexpressing the RAC2P29L1-45 substrate (despite ~5-fold higher expression than the direct epitope construct), while a linear RAC2P29L-specific TCR readily recognized the same cells, indicating the spliced epitope is not generated in vivo at immunologically relevant levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C53 provide strong evidence from multiple cell systems (Mel21a and NIH-HHD) and controls (Figures 5B-E). The positive recognition by linear-specific TCR (C49-C50) excludes antigen presentation defects, while qPCR confirms substrate overexpression (C52). The consistent negative results with splice-specific TCR despite overexpression strongly support the conclusion that in vivo generation is insufficient for T cell recognition.

results.result: The authors conclude that available algorithms and in vitro PCPS reactions do not reliably simulate in vivo splicing for neo-splicetope identification, and recommend mandatory proof of cell surface presentation before TCR generation, arguing against general applicability of algorithm-driven reverse immunology pipelines for neo-splicetopes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C54-C57 represent the main conclusions drawn from the negative experimental results with both KRASG12V and RAC2P29L. These inferences are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence showing discordance between in vitro and in vivo results. The recommendation (C56) is a logical consequence of the findings, though it represents a methodological proposal rather than an experimental result.

results.result: High-quality peptide synthesis reaches only 95-99% purity, and even minor amounts of faulty peptide substrates can become prevalent in in vitro splicing reactions because spliced peptide generation is significantly less efficient than non-spliced peptide generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 combine established knowledge about peptide synthesis quality with experimental observations (Figure 4A, Figure 3—figure supplement 5B) showing the relative inefficiency of splicing. This represents an important methodological insight explaining how synthesis artifacts can confound in vitro PCPS experiments. The logic is sound and supported by the data.

results.result: High substrate and proteasome concentrations used in in vitro PCPS may force splicing reactions that do not or only inefficiently occur under in vivo conditions where single substrate proteins are processed.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is explicitly presented as speculation ('One possible explanation') to explain the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results. While this is a reasonable hypothesis consistent with the data, it lacks direct experimental support. The authors appropriately frame this as speculative rather than demonstrated.

results.result: Prior work established that purified 20S proteasomes with synthetic substrates reproduce in vivo epitope generation with high fidelity for non-spliced epitopes, that proteasomes can generate spliced epitopes via reverse proteolysis, and that in vitro PCPS reactions mimicked in vivo splicing for several previously characterized splicetopes.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C11 accurately summarize prior literature (supported by appropriate citations) establishing the foundation for the current study. These claims represent established knowledge in the field and provide important context for understanding why the negative results in this study are significant and unexpected.

results.result: Recent literature suggests the amount of cell surface-presented spliced epitopes is considerably less than initially estimated, and the abundance of spliced epitopes is a matter of substantial controversy.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 accurately represent the current state of the field based on cited literature (Mylonas et al., 2018; Rolfs et al., 2019; Liepe et al., 2016, 2019; Paes et al., 2019). These claims provide important context showing the authors' findings align with emerging concerns in the field about spliced epitope abundance.

results.result: Epitope generation efficiency depends on epitope sequence, surrounding protein sequence, and proteasomal cleavage properties. Current algorithms for predicting non-spliced epitopes are insufficient for large-scale reverse immunology, and algorithms for spliced epitopes based on protein sequence and cleavage properties do not yet exist. In vitro proteasome digestion with mass spectrometry remains the standard validation tool.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 accurately summarize the current state of the field based on appropriate citations. These claims provide essential background explaining the limitations of computational approaches and the rationale for experimental validation, contextualizing why the authors' negative findings are significant.

results.result: PCPS of cancer-driving antigens could generate attractive neoepitopes for TCR-based adoptive T cell therapy.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is explicitly speculative ('could generate') and represents the initial hypothesis motivating the study. The subsequent experimental results actually argue against this possibility for the specific cases tested, though the claim itself is appropriately framed as potential rather than demonstrated.

results.result: KRAS is frequently mutated in cancer with G12V being common in pancreatic, colon, and lung cancers, but G12X mutations do not produce high-affinity HLA-A*02:01 binding linear epitopes. RAC2P29L is a driver mutation, and the linear RAC2P29L epitope has predicted IC50 of 2 nM.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C15, C40-C41 represent established knowledge about these cancer-associated mutations. Claims C14 and C42 are computational predictions that are appropriately qualified. These claims provide essential background justifying the focus on spliced epitopes as an alternative approach.

results.result: TCRs generated in ABabDII mice specifically recognized the respective target peptides with high efficacy.
results.evaluation: Claim C3 is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, demonstrating peptide-specific recognition. However, this claim is somewhat redundant with the more detailed Result 1 and represents a general summary statement.

results.result: The authors failed to detect neo-splicetope-specific T cell responses when testing in vivo generation, and only the RAC2P29L-derived neo-splicetope was generated by in vitro PCPS.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 represent high-level summary statements of the main negative findings that are detailed in other results. These are accurate summaries supported by the comprehensive experimental data, but are better captured in the more specific results above.
